comments.body:
One more for the same change: who may run commands from a comment at all. Today pr-agent never checks the commenter (`DefaultIdentityProvider.verify_eligibility` always returns `ELIGIBLE`, and only the GitHub and Bitbucket apps call it), so on a public repo any GitHub user can run every enabled command on the operator's key. Our own `pr-agent-review.yaml` already limits comment commands to write access (#4002). Proposal:

6. Commands from a PR comment run only when the commenter has write access, checked through a provider capability (collaborator permission on GitHub and Gitea, Developer or above on GitLab, repository permission on Bitbucket). Where a provider cannot check, comment commands are refused unless the operator opts out with a host-only setting. Automatic runs on PR events are unchanged.

I'd like to take item 5 as a standalone first step, if that's useful while the rest of the direction is being decided.

The host-only lists in `config_security.py` only say what's blocked, so a new `configuration.toml` key is open to comment overrides by default, with nothing prompting a decision (#4443 is the example you mentioned). I'd add a unit test in the style of `test_config_dead_keys.py`: it walks every key in `configuration.toml` and fails unless the key is either rejected by the existing checks or listed in a new explicit set of keys that are still accepted from comments.

That set would start as a snapshot of today's behaviour, so nothing changes at runtime and no existing command breaks. It just means a new key can't stay open unless someone chooses that in the diff. The same set could later feed the review of what should stay comment-settable, or the opt-in list in item 3.

Two questions before I start:
1. Are you happy for this to land ahead of the wider change, or would you rather it wait for the review of the direction?
2. Should the set live in `config_security.py` next to the host-only lists, or in the test as a ledger?

Thanks for offering, and for scoping it so nothing changes at runtime. Yes, please go ahead of the wider change: a snapshot test only makes the next new key a visible choice. Keep the accepted set in the test as a ledger for now; nothing at runtime would read it yet, and item 3 can move it into `config_security.py` once it has a reader.

comments.body:
Thanks for the explicit acceptance criteria and the honest no-production-claims framing. Having dug deeper, I don't think we should take this now.

Selecting prior answers by visible content reopens the hole we measured on #2722, and filtering by bot authorship does not close it here either: every Ask answer embeds the asker's raw question verbatim (pr_questions.py:134, the same echo as #2629), and anyone who can comment can run /ask, so the history is seedable with hostile text even when every comment in it is bot-authored. Your untrusted-context marking is the right instinct but the weakest mitigation, since the model still reads the text.

So this trades a real injection surface for an ergonomic gain, with no demand recorded yet. Marking it blocked and leaving it open for reactions; if demand shows up, a design needs bot-author filtering plus the history handled as untrusted, both as hard requirements.

comments.body:
Confirmed there is nothing like this today: no CI feedback tool in `pr_agent/tools/`, no matching command in the dispatch map, nothing in the docs. The GitLab webhook also only branches on `merge_request` and `note` object kinds, so pipeline events are dropped entirely and would need a new branch, and fetching job logs would be new surface on each provider.

There is a workaround that may cover part of your case now. `--extra_config_url` (added in #2406) accepts a bare local path to a `.pr_agent.toml`, and `extra_instructions` from it reaches the review prompt. So a CI job can write a toml summarising the failed jobs and invoke pr-agent with `--extra_config_url=./ci_context.toml`. You avoid the waiting problem by inverting the trigger: run pr-agent as a later CI job that declares `needs:` on the build jobs, rather than from the MR webhook.

That is off-label, since the flag exists to merge config rather than inject context, and it does none of the "is this failure related to the change" classification you are asking for. Worth a maintainer's view on appetite for the real thing.

Since my last comment I've designed this properly, and I'd like a maintainer read on appetite before writing any code.

Shape: a provider-side CI evidence reader plus deterministic signal extraction, surfaced as a section of the existing `/review` rather than as a new command — the review comment already has the persistent-comment and dedup machinery, and enrich-the-review changes have a better landing record here than new tools.

For the 65-job case: failures get deduplicated by error signature, so one root cause across twelve jobs is one finding with a count rather than twelve. On relatedness I'd deliberately stop short of QtCIAnalysisBot's "unrelated, restage recommended" — the best published flaky-test classifier sits at F1 0.66, and a confidently wrong "unrelated" is how a bot gets muted. It reports what you'd judge from instead: file overlap between the diff and the failing job, and whether the same signature hit unrelated jobs.

One thing beyond the ask: the same reader flags dangerous *green* pipelines, e.g. a Terraform plan with resources to destroy. Everything comparable only fires on red.

GitLab lands alongside GitHub rather than after it — pipeline events need one webhook branch and a project checkbox.

@naorpeled — is this something you'd take? Happy to send it as small independent PRs, evidence layer first.

Correcting my own comment from 14-08: I said there was nothing like this today and that was wrong.

[artifacts] already exists, in configuration.toml lines 481 to 493. It reads a local file and appends it to extra_instructions for pr_reviewer, pr_description and pr_code_suggestions, truncating at max_artifact_size, default 50000 characters. It is documented under "CI artifact context" in docs/docs/installation/github.md. I ran load_artifact() against a build log and it produced the labelled block as advertised. It is a much better fit than the extra_config_url workaround I suggested, so please ignore that.

Two catches for your case. It is wired only into github_action_runner.py, so a GitLab webhook cannot reach it, and it makes no relatedness judgement and no dedup across jobs. The 65-job classification you asked for is still unbuilt.

@naorpeled the appetite question stands.

While this waits for v1, data from a consumer-side pilot (GitLab, 0.46.0, `[artifacts]` plus a review job that runs last in the pipeline). On 10 MRs whose pipeline failed and whose next commit fixed it, a blind judge found `/review` named the exact cause in 0 of 10 from the diff alone and in 5 of 10 with log tails, and every review with logs at least flagged the failure. Unrelated findings fell from 14 to 7.

Lessons for a native version: take the end of each log, redact before truncating, ask for a block-scalar field, exclude the reviewer's own job, and keep it opt-in.

The hardening it relies on can land before v1: #3972 (#3978), #3973, #3975 (#3976), #3982, #3983, #3984.

Thanks for bearing with this, @misery. Since v0.48.0 most of it works without new code. On GitLab CI:

- Run the review as the last job (`stage: .post`, `when: always`, so red pipelines are covered and green ones with planned destroys too).
- Have a job before it write the tail of each job log to one file, and point `ARTIFACT_PATH` at it with `artifacts__truncate_from=end`. The log is marked untrusted and common credentials are redacted first.
- Use `ARTIFACT_INSTRUCTIONS` to ask `/review` for an extra field such as `pipeline_status` (failed jobs and why, failed tests, planned destroys); since #3998 it renders as its own row in the review comment.
- Build jobs need `artifacts: when: always`, as GitLab uploads only on success by default.

The pr-agent side is the same on every provider, but the CI wiring differs: on GitHub Actions it is a final job with `needs:` and `if: always()`, with the logs passed via `actions/upload-artifact`. Fetching the logs for you, deduplicating one cause across jobs and a related-or-flaky verdict are still unbuilt; keeping this open for that after v1.

title: Support analysis of CI build logs

comments.body:
Hey @aleen42,
Thanks for opening this issue, I'm not familiar with codegraph, will need to do some research 👀 

What would you expect the interface of integrating it with pr-agent to look like?

> Hey [@aleen42](https://github.com/aleen42), Thanks for opening this issue, I'm not familiar with codegraph, will need to do some research 👀
> 
> What would you expect the interface of integrating it with pr-agent to look like?


IMO a full codegraph index may not be a great fit for pr-agent's scenario. pr-agent processes one PR at a time, so even if you build a whole-repo index, the utilization would be pretty low — most of the indexed data is irrelevant to a single PR's diff, yet you'd still pay the cost of building and maintaining the index.

That said, there's a more targeted optimization that works well here: instead of indexing the entire repo, use a tool like tree-sitter to parse only the code related to the PR's changes and extract the relevant call chain on the fly. You then feed that call chain into the LLM as part of the prompt. This gives the model the cross-function context it needs to reason beyond the diff, while keeping the analysis scoped and cheap — no heavyweight repo-wide index required.

Worth noting what already exists, since it sits between the two positions here. pr-agent already expands each hunk beyond the diff: `allow_dynamic_context` (`configuration.toml:42`) walks back up to `max_extra_lines_before_dynamic_context` lines until it hits an enclosing function or class, with `patch_extra_lines_before/after` as the static fallback.

So the cheap end of what @victorljii describes is already in place. What is missing is following the call chain out of the changed file, which is exactly the part a tree-sitter pass or an index would add, and also where the cost lands: dynamic context is line based and needs no extra tooling, while anything call-graph aware brings a per-language parser and somewhere to keep it. There is no extension point for either today, so it would mean changes in the diff assembly path rather than a plugin.

I agree that building and maintaining a full repo or even multi-repo graph for every PR probably isn’t worth the cost.

This reminded me of a similar solution I tried in one of my projects with [Graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify).

Based on that experience, PR-Agent could query an existing graph only for the functions, methods and classes touched by the diff. This could provide context without rebuilding the full graph for every PR.

It updates only the affected part of the graph and does it deterministically. It already supports parsers for many languages so may be worth trying for this use case.

Yes, it is. We can try to index code outside diffs via existed graphs, but not try to build it for users since it may result it a payload. According to my daily uses of Codex, it also use it as its strategy to find references.
I mainly wanted to share Graphify as a project that might be relevant to this use case. I’ll leave it to the maintainers to decide whether it could be a good fit for PR-Agent.

Graphify looks like a reasonable fit for the shape this thread converged on: query an existing graph for only the symbols the diff touches.

You can prototype exactly that today, in a pipeline, with no changes here. Run the graph step yourself, scope the extract to the diff, and pass it in as `extra_instructions`: it is a plain setting, so `PR_REVIEWER__EXTRA_INSTRUCTIONS` (or `PR_CODE_SUGGESTIONS__EXTRA_INSTRUCTIONS`) from the CI environment lands verbatim in the system prompt. I checked that end to end. Note `repo_context_files` will not do it: it reads through the provider API rather than from disk, so anything it loads has to be committed first.

What that does not give you is pr-agent doing the scoping itself, which is the part that needs a decision: whether it ever owns a parser or only consumes one supplied externally, and if externally whether that arrives over MCP (#2348, open but conflicting and untouched since April) or a config-declared context provider.

I would rather see a pipeline prototype and its results before we settle that. It turns a design argument into an evidence one.

Thanks for the Graphify pointer, oleksii-tumanov; querying an existing graph for only the symbols a diff touches is still the shape I think this lands in.

Update on the MCP half, since I pointed at #2348 in August. It is closed: the branch sat in an organization fork, so only the author could rebase it. The approach carries forward as #2944 with stdio and the JSON envelope dropped, and #2944 is parked until after v1, so nothing arrives over MCP in the near term.

None of that settles whether pr-agent ever owns a parser, so the pipeline prototype is still the useful next step. The `extra_instructions` route from my 28 August comment needs no changes on our side.

Disclosure: I maintain [trace-mcp](https://github.com/nikolai-vysotskyi/trace-mcp), an MCP server that does diff-scoped graph context packaging for agent code reviews.

We ran that pipeline measurement over 60 merged bug-fix PRs across 6 public repositories (comparing naive "diff + touched source files" against diff-scoped symbol bundles). Three concrete findings from that benchmark that are relevant to the `extra_instructions` prototype:

1. **The line-shift trap when mapping diffs to symbols.** If you take `+new` line numbers from `git diff --unified=0 <since>..<until>` hunk headers and overlap them against AST spans stored in an index, the mapping silently breaks unless the index was built at that exact commit. If the graph was built against the default branch or a dirty worktree, line shifts will map hunks to the wrong enclosing functions, producing confident context about unrelated code without throwing an error. A freshness assertion (comparing commit SHAs before running the resolver) is necessary.

2. **Scoping to changed symbols alone loses caller context.** In our early runs, packaging only the modified symbol definitions caused the reviewer model to hallucinate caller assumptions and miss ripple effects. Conversely, expanding full transitive dependents blew past token budgets. The middle ground that preserved review comprehension was:
   - Direct definition + immediate imports for each changed symbol.
   - 1-hop inbound callers/dependents for impact assessment.
   - A hard token budget ceiling on the assembled block.

3. **Measured token vs quality trade-off.** On those 60 PRs, diff-scoped symbol packaging yielded a median 72.7% reduction in prompt tokens compared to loading full touched files, while bug-fix comprehension remained at parity (67% vs 65%).

Thanks for disclosing the interest up front, and for bringing numbers.

Your first finding lands here whatever we adopt, because we hit the same class independently: `repo_context.py` keys its cache with no revision on a 15 minute TTL (#3119), so a push to the base branch inside that window serves content from a commit that has moved. #3148 and #3149 are both fixing it, so that assertion is a precondition we owe anyway rather than a graph concern. Your second finding is the part this thread had not settled: we agreed on diff-scoped symbols but never on how far to expand, and one hop inbound with a hard ceiling is a sharper answer than anything here.

On 67% against 65% of 60 PRs, that is one PR either way, so I read it as no measured difference rather than parity. The prototype is still what would move this: run the packaging yourself and pass it in through `extra_instructions`, which needs nothing from us.

Nothing arrives over MCP before v1: #2944 is closed in favour of Discussion #3147, where the runtime choice is open.

Thanks for the detailed reply, and for the pointers to #3119, #3148/#3149 and #3147.

Fair on 67 vs 65 — with n=60 that is one PR either way, so no measured difference is the honest reading, not parity.

Good to know the revision-keyed cache is already being fixed on your side, and that #2944 closed toward #3147 — that tells me where MCP-side work would land.

The extra_instructions path needs nothing from you, so I've logged the prototype on our side and will run it there. If it produces numbers worth this thread, I'll bring them back; if not, it stays our experiment.

Revisiting this, since one thing changed since September: `[artifacts]` now gives a pipeline a proper slot for this kind of context, better than the `extra_instructions` route I suggested. The content is marked as untrusted, common credentials are redacted, and it reaches `/review`, `/improve`, `/describe` and `/ask` from the GitHub Action or the CLI. So a CI step can run Graphify, trace-mcp or a tree-sitter pass scoped to the diff (changed symbols, their imports and one hop of callers, under a token cap, as @nikolai-vysotskyi measured) and pass the result with `ARTIFACT_PATH`. Build the graph at the PR head commit, or the line numbers drift.

Two pieces would make it first-class, both open to anyone: a docs recipe for this, and #4335, accepting more than one artifact so graph context can sit next to CI logs (#2640). @nikolai-vysotskyi, if your prototype ran, numbers from this route would be welcome here. pr-agent owning a parser stays a post-v1 call in #3147.

Numbers from the `[artifacts]` route, measured on this repo's own reviews. We replayed v0.48.0's `/review` at 26 reviewed PR commits holding 55 findings maintainers raised, with each PR's real description and linked issue, and scored the outputs blind (two judge pools, 212 of 220 verdicts agreed, every quote verified):

- A diff-scoped tree-sitter bundle (changed symbols, callers, similar code, sibling files, tests that exercise the change) plus a short instruction on how to read it raised the score from 15.5 to 20.75 of 55 with a Sonnet answerer and from 16.75 to 22 with Opus. Noise flags stayed at zero, and it adds no model call.
- The extra catches are a mix, led by missing or vacuous tests, then callers, a duplicated helper and an unfixed sibling. The bundle runs also lost a few findings the plain runs caught, so +5 is the net.
- Caveats: Claude stood in for gpt-6.1-sol, there was a single run per arm, and the bundle's sections were shaped on earlier misses from this repo.

Since it already works through `ARTIFACT_PATH`, I'd suggest trying it in this repo's self-review workflow first, with the builder as a script next to `scripts/structural_reach_producer.py` rather than inside pr-agent. The builder and its instructions are on a branch of my fork, [`scripts/review_context`](https://github.com/IsmaelMartinez/pr-agent/tree/review-context-builder/scripts/review_context), as a starting point: it covers any language with a tree-sitter tags query, and the README lists the hardening it still needs before it sees untrusted PRs. @naorpeled @ofir-frd, does that split work for you, keeping a built-in parser as the post-v1 question in #3147?

If you want to check this on your own repo first, it runs locally against any PR you can read, with no change to your pipeline. You need `pip install "pr-agent[github]"` 0.49.0 or later, `GITHUB__USER_TOKEN` and a model key such as `OPENAI__KEY`, and a clone of your repo on the PR branch with `origin/main` fetched (full history, not `--depth 1`):

```bash
git clone --depth 1 -b review-context-builder https://github.com/IsmaelMartinez/pr-agent /tmp/rc
uv run --no-project --with tree-sitter-language-pack==1.22.1 python /tmp/rc/scripts/review_context/graph_bundle_ts.py \
  --repo "$PWD" --base origin/main --head HEAD --pr 123 --out-dir /tmp/review-context --generic

# the same review without and with the bundle, written to JSON instead of the PR
pr-agent --pr_url https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/123 --json-output before.json review --config.publish_output=false
ARTIFACT_PATH=/tmp/review-context/pr123.G6.md \
ARTIFACT_INSTRUCTIONS="$(cat /tmp/rc/scripts/review_context/instructions.txt)" \
ARTIFACTS__TARGET_TOOLS='["pr_reviewer"]' \
pr-agent --pr_url https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/123 --json-output after.json review --config.publish_output=false
```

Then compare the key issues in the two files. One run each is noisy, so try a few PRs where you already know what a reviewer found. The builder never runs PR code and reads only regular files tracked in git at the head commit, skipping secret-named and oversized ones; an independent security review of it is still to come.

On our side, we will wire it into this repo's self-review workflow and check it on live PRs, tracked in #4763; results will go there. @aleen42, this is similar in spirit to what you asked about (repository context from a code graph), though built per PR with tree-sitter rather than from a codegraph index.

I also compared bundles on our own PRs, and this one scored highest of those we tried, ahead of a Graphify-based bundle. In an earlier round, before the PR description and issue were in the prompt, and with each given its own reading instruction, Opus caught 21 + 5 partial of the 55 with it against 17 + 4 with Graphify's. The difference is probably down to its similar-code, sibling-file and tests sections, which Graphify's graph does not produce.
